title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1: Hilary and Faustus; then Arminius/Arnoldus reject the grace that makes the good will — only sweet persuasion, event to free will
pass_a_gloss: So Hilary in the Epistle to Augustine. That testimony, As he has dealt to every man the measure of faith, and the like, they will to have avail unto this, that he who has begun to will is helped, not that it is also given that he may will. A little after, They render the reason of elect or rejected from this, that unto each the merit of his own will is joined. Finally Faustus of Riez, the Semipelagians’ coryphaeus, It is of Divine pity, he says, that thou art called, but committed unto thy will that thou follow, Pag. 1493. God waits for the will of him who is to be purged, Pag. 1506. Innumerable of this kind occur in this author, from which we gather that Pelagians and Semipelagians conspired in this, that they never willed to grant God’s special munificence and mercy by which faith and charity are infused into some, and a good will is thereby created in the same. Now in the place of a makeweight we will also set this: that Arminius and Arnoldus, and the rest who have come forth from the same School, do not acknowledge that which the Pelagians and Semipelagians exploded, namely that which by its efficacy makes the good will; but only that which by persuasion moves that it may will to be good, but commits the event unto free will itself.
pass_b_english: So Hilary to Augustine: texts like As he has dealt to each the measure of faith they take to mean the one who has begun to will is helped—not that willing itself is given. A little later: they explain elect and rejected by the merit of each one’s own will joined on. Faustus of Riez, the Semipelagians’ chief, says (p. 1493): It is of divine pity that you are called, but left to your will that you follow; and (p. 1506): God waits for the will of the one to be purged. From countless such lines we gather Pelagians and Semipelagians agreed never to grant God’s special munificence by which faith and charity are poured into some and a good will is thereby created in them. For a makeweight add this: Arminius, Arnoldus, and the rest from that school do not acknowledge the grace Pelagians and Semipelagians rejected—the grace that by its efficacy makes the good will—but only the grace that by persuasion moves the will to want to be good, and leaves the event to free will.
source_text: Sic Hilarius in Epist. ad August. Illud testimonium, Sicut unicuique partitus est mensuram fidei, et similia, ad id volunt valere, ut adjuvetur qui coeperit velle, non ut etiam donetur ut velit. Paulo post, Rationem reddunt electorum vel rejectorum ex eo, quod unicuique meritum propriae voluntatis adjungitur. Denique Faustus Rhegiensis Semipelagianorum coryphaeus, Divinae, inquit, miserationis est ut voceris, sed tuae voluntati commissum ut sequaris, Pag. 1493. Voluntatem ejus qui est purgandus exspectat Deus, Pag. 1506. Hujusmodi innumera apud hunc auctorem occurrunt, ex quibus colligimus Pelagianos et Semipelagianos in hoc conspirasse, quod numquam concedere voluerunt specialem Dei munificentiam et misericordiam, qua infundatur fides et charitas aliquibus, bonaque voluntas eo pacto in iisdem creetur. Jam superpondii loco et illud apponemus: Arminium ac Arnoldum, caeterosque qui ex eadem Schola prodierunt, non agnoscere illam quam Pelagiani et Semipelagiani exploserunt, nempe illam quae sua efficacitate bonam voluntatem facit; sed illam solam quae suasione movet ut bona esse velit, eventum autem ipsi libero arbitrio commitit.
